newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Chances of immediate NZ easing remote - BTNZ.
newsitem.headline: Chances of immediate NZ easing remote - BTNZ.

text.p: Bankers Trust New Zealand said on Thursday the chances of an official easing of monetary conditions at next week's release of the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Statement were slim.
But BTNZ said that in the short term, the fiscal parameters set by the new coalition government should allow the RBNZ to endorse a market-led easing.
BTNZ economists said in a commentary that from the market's perspective, compared to policy that existed before the coalition deal, the new programme was a backward step.
"Inflation and taxes will be higher and spending discipline looser. In addition, the role of Winston Peters as Treasurer may be viewed with some concern."
But BTNZ said that comparison was "not all that fair".

The election result guaranteed policy would change and that Winston Peters would play a major role in the new government, but what was at stake during the coalition negotiation phase was the extent of the change.

"The econonic direction of New Zealand remains broadly intact. Most importantly the Reserve Bank Act has not been changed," BTNZ said. "The RBNZ remains independent and its sole focus is the maintenance of price stability."
Meanwhile, the government had retained its commitment to running surpluses and repaying debt.
"There are no changes to rules on foreign investment, other than for rural land, and reductions in tariffs remain on track."
There had been big changes in social policy, particularly health.
While the associated spending was significant, BTNZ pointed out that National had increased spending on goods and services by more than NZ$1 billion in each of the last two fiscal years.

"Indeed, if the fiscal parameters in each year are stuck to, then the increase in spending over the three years may actually turn out to be less than would have occurred under a National government," BTNZ said.

"In the the short term, the fiscal parameters should allow the RBNZ to endorse a market led easing in monetary conditions next week. We doubt the RBNZ will ease further until it has seen the December quarter CPI at least."
BTNZ said the key to the coalition will be whether it stands the test of time.

"Tension between the two partners has the potential to be disruptive to the policy programme. This will have costs in the form of uncertainty and lack of confidence among businesses and households. It will also impact on the bond market."
But BTNZ said there seemed to be little reason for New Zealand bonds to trade much below Australian yields.
"We still see potential for outperformance against the U.S. over the early part of 1997," the bank added.
